sections.heading: Coming to the task weak and dependent
sections.text: Lord God, I have been asked to preach today, and I come to it feeling how weak and needy I am. I do not want to stand up in my own confidence or fill the time with my own thoughts. I want your truth to build people up, and I want my words to be an honest witness to you. Please help me as I preach and as I pray. Lift my heart toward you, and give me the help of your Spirit, not so I can seem impressive, but so Christ can be seen and your people can be served.
theological_themes: Preaching as witness to divine truth
The Spirit's help in prayer and proclamation

scripture_references.connection: Paul says ministry competence does not come from ourselves but from God, who makes his servants able to minister the new covenant. That directly supports the prayer’s confession of weakness and request for divine help.
Peter frames speaking ministry as service done by God’s strength, so that God receives glory. This grounds the desire to preach in dependence rather than self-display.

sections.heading: Asking for clarity, truth, and a living sense of what I preach
sections.text: Bring to mind what truly belongs to the message. Give me enough substance, clear thought, fitting words, and a steady freedom to speak. Keep the truth from staying only in my head; make it real to my own heart as I say it. Help me speak in a way that reaches consciences—carefully, honestly, and with love—so that people are not merely informed, but brought before you.
theological_themes: Illumination and clarity in handling God’s Word
Truth felt personally before being spoken publicly

scripture_references.connection: Paul asks for an open door and for clarity in making the mystery of Christ known. This fits the prayer’s request for freedom, fitting words, and clear proclamation.
Paul charges Timothy to handle the word of truth rightly. The prayer’s concern not to speak vaguely or carelessly reflects that same responsibility.

sections.heading: Keeping me humble while I serve
sections.text: Keep me aware of my limits the whole time. If anything goes well, do not let me admire myself or replay my performance with pride. Let me be glad only that your truth was served. Make me faithful enough to point people to you, and sober enough to warn those who are ignoring your mercy that they cannot treat your grace as a small thing.
theological_themes: God’s mercy must not be neglected

scripture_references.connection: Paul insists that ministers proclaim Christ rather than themselves and that the treasure is carried in fragile vessels so the power is seen to belong to God. This undergirds both humility and confidence in preaching.
Hebrews warns against drifting from and neglecting the salvation God has announced. This supports the prayer’s sober desire that hearers not dismiss God’s mercy without accountability.

sections.heading: Speaking both warning and comfort
sections.text: Give me freedom to speak to the real sorrows of your people. Help me name grief, fear, weariness, guilt, and temptation truthfully, and then set before them the comforts you have actually given in Christ. Wake up those who are spiritually dull or distracted. Let the truth preached come with your power, so that your people are refreshed, softened, convicted, and comforted as they need.
theological_themes: Pastoral preaching for wounded and wandering people
Conviction and comfort through God’s Word
God’s power accompanying the preached truth

scripture_references.connection: Paul tells Timothy to preach the word with readiness, including reproof, rebuke, exhortation, and patience. This supports the prayer’s balance of warning, conviction, and comfort.

Paul thanks God that the preached word was received as God’s word and was at work in believers. This grounds the request that the sermon be attended with divine power rather than remain mere human speech.
Isaiah’s commission includes speaking comfort to God’s people after judgment and sorrow. It gives biblical shape to the preacher’s desire to address affliction with God-given consolation.

sections.heading: Preaching Christ so people become holy
sections.text: Help me press the strongest and truest reasons for holiness: that the Son of God came in our flesh, suffered, died, and gave himself for sinners. Do not let me handle the cross coldly or harshly. Give me warmth, seriousness, tenderness, and holy urgency, so that Christ’s death is shown in its purpose and beauty, and people are drawn away from sin toward him.
theological_themes: Christ’s incarnation and suffering as the heart of the message
The cross as both mercy and call to holiness
Preaching Christ with warmth and reverence

scripture_references.connection: Paul connects saving grace in Christ with training believers to renounce ungodliness and live holy lives. This directly supports the prayer’s desire to use Christ’s giving of himself as the great argument for holiness.

Peter presents Christ’s suffering not only as bearing sin but also as bringing believers into a new life of righteousness. That matches the prayer’s link between Christ’s sufferings and moral transformation.
John testifies that the eternal Word became flesh and revealed divine glory. This supports the prayer’s appeal to Christ’s incarnation as central to the preacher’s proclamation.

sections.heading: Being made fit for the work and kept close to you
sections.text: I need you myself—your support, comfort, strength, and holiness. Make my life a clean and willing channel for your grace, so that I may truly serve you and do some good for your people. Refresh me as I serve among them. Do not let me treat glorious truth in a thin or careless way, or give a damaged witness to such a worthy Redeemer. Keep my heart in step with you while I do this work.
theological_themes: The minister’s own need for grace and holiness
Communion with God in the work of ministry

scripture_references.connection: Paul tells Timothy to watch both his life and his teaching, showing that the preacher’s character and doctrine belong together. This supports the prayer’s concern to be made holy and useful, not merely skillful.
Jesus teaches that fruitful service depends on abiding in him, because apart from him his disciples can do nothing. This grounds the closing plea to stay in tune with God while working.
Paul describes proclaiming Christ with the aim of maturity, while laboring with God’s energy. This reflects the prayer’s longing to serve effectively through divine strength.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase about leaving sinners 'inexcusable' is theologically weighty and could sound like the preacher wants to condemn people. I rendered it as a sober warning that people cannot neglect God’s mercy as though it were insignificant, preserving accountability without implying cruelty.

The original calls the audience 'slothful,' which may be pastorally sharp and culturally direct. I kept the substance as spiritual dullness and distraction without making the preacher contemptuous of the congregation.

The term 'unction' can carry different connotations across Christian traditions. I expressed it as the help and power of the Holy Spirit in preaching, which is broadly biblical and faithful to the prayer’s intent.
The original uses 'men' generically for hearers. I rendered it as 'people' to preserve the intended scope without changing the meaning.
significant_interpretive_choices: I treated 'freedom' in preaching as Spirit-given liberty, clarity, and readiness to speak, rather than as personal spontaneity or emotional release alone.
I interpreted 'open the sorrows of thy people' as naming and addressing the real burdens of believers with biblical comfort, not as exposing private suffering publicly.
I rendered 'pure channel of thy grace' as a life that is clean and willing for God’s service, avoiding any implication that the minister mediates grace in a priestly or sacramental sense.

I kept the original movement from personal weakness, to preaching help, to humility, to warning and comfort for hearers, to Christ-centered holiness, and finally to the minister’s own need for grace and communion with God.
